sections.overview: Cymothoa exigua is a marine isopod assigned to the fish-parasitic family Cymothoidae.
sections.identification: The flattened, segmented crustacean has hooked legs for anchoring; females occupy the mouth while males have been found on the gills.
sections.habitat: It parasitizes marine fishes in the eastern Pacific, including the spotted rose snapper Lutjanus guttatus.
sections.diet: In two infected snappers, more than 90% of the tongue was absent. The authors proposed that the isopod might help hold food in the mouth, but did not demonstrate functional replacement.
sections.behavior: A Honduran survey recorded it on two fish hosts in the Gulf of Fonseca, with specimens attached in the mouth or on the gills.
sections.reproduction: Species-specific reproductive stages are poorly documented; cymothoid females generally brood developing embryos in a ventral marsupium.
sections.ecology: It is one of many fish-parasitic isopods, but its buccal attachment and reported tongue atrophy distinguish it from gill- and skin-attaching relatives.
sections.conservation: The cited field observations document hosts and attachment, not a population trend.
